subsection: 1. Employee rights and responsibilities: legislative and non-legislative protection

notes.h: Pay and the national minimum wage
notes.b: Pay protection in Irish law combines a legal floor on hourly rates with rules on how and when wages are paid.
points: The National Minimum Wage Act 2000 sets a legal minimum hourly rate, and an employer cannot pay a worker less than the rate that applies.
The minimum rate is reviewed by the government, usually after recommendations from the Low Pay Commission, and each change affects employers' costs and workers' take-home pay.
The Payment of Wages Act 1991 requires employers to pay wages on time and to give employees a written statement of pay and deductions.
Deductions from wages are allowed only where the law permits them or where the employee has agreed to them in writing.
A worker who is not paid properly can make a complaint to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).
The Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 limits average weekly working hours and guarantees rest breaks, daily and weekly rest periods, and annual leave.
The Terms of Employment (Information) Acts require employers to give employees a written statement of core terms, such as pay, hours and place of work.

The Employment (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2018 bans zero-hours contracts in most cases, guarantees a minimum payment when an employee is called in but not given the expected work, and provides for banded hours after a period of regular working.
The Sick Leave Act 2022 gives eligible employees a statutory right to paid sick leave, with the number of paid days set in law.
The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 gives employees a right to request flexible or remote working and extends leave for family and carers.
The Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 is the main law on workplace safety in Ireland, and it is enforced by the Health and Safety Authority (HSA).
Employers must identify hazards, assess risks, prepare a safety statement, and provide training, information and safe equipment.
Employees must take reasonable care of their own safety and that of others, use the protective equipment provided, and report hazards and accidents.
An employee who reasonably believes that work poses a serious and imminent risk can refuse to do it, and cannot be penalised for doing so.
Breaches of the Act can lead to prosecution, so safety duties are enforceable obligations and not just good practice.

notes.b: The Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015 protect employees and job applicants from discrimination in the workplace.
points: The Acts cover recruitment, pay, training, promotion, conditions of employment and dismissal.
The nine protected grounds are gender, civil status, family status, sexual orientation, religion, age, disability, race, and membership of the Traveller community.
Race includes colour, nationality and ethnic or national origins.

Direct discrimination means a person is treated less favourably because of a protected ground, while indirect discrimination means a rule that applies to everyone disadvantages people on a ground, unless it is objectively justified.
An employer must provide reasonable accommodation for a disabled employee, unless doing so would be a disproportionate burden.
Discrimination claims are made to the Workplace Relations Commission.
The Unfair Dismissals Acts 1977 to 2015 protect employees with the required length of service from being dismissed unfairly.
A dismissal is fair only if it is for a reason such as capability, conduct, redundancy or a legal prohibition, and the employer follows fair procedures.
Some reasons, such as trade union membership or raising a safety complaint, make a dismissal automatically unfair.
Constructive dismissal occurs when an employee resigns because the employer's conduct makes continued employment unreasonable, and the law treats the resignation as a dismissal.
Redress for unfair dismissal may be reinstatement, re-engagement or compensation, decided by the WRC or the Labour Court.
The WRC investigates and adjudicates on many employment complaints, including pay, discrimination, dismissal and working time claims.
The Labour Court hears appeals from WRC decisions and handles certain industrial relations disputes.
Employees usually must make a complaint within a set time limit, so acting promptly protects the claim.
Employees must follow reasonable and lawful instructions from their employer and attend work as rostered.
Employees owe a duty of good faith, which includes not disclosing confidential business information and not competing unfairly with the employer.
When resigning, employees must give the notice required by their contract or by law.

notes.b: Protection also comes from agreements and procedures that sit alongside the law.
points: An employment contract sets out the express terms agreed by employer and employee, and sits alongside statutory rights, which cannot be signed away.
A collective agreement is negotiated between a trade union and an employer, and sets pay and conditions for a group of workers.
HR policies in a staff handbook set expected conduct and procedures, and they cannot reduce statutory rights.
Codes of practice, such as the Labour Relations Commission code on grievance and disciplinary procedures, give practical guidance that bodies such as the WRC take into account.
A grievance procedure lets an employee raise a complaint informally and then formally, through a set sequence of steps.

keyTerms.definition: A legal minimum hourly rate that employers must pay workers, set under the National Minimum Wage Act 2000.
A resignation forced by the employer's conduct, which the law treats as a dismissal.
Less favourable treatment of a person because of a protected ground, such as age or race.
A rule or practice that applies to everyone but disadvantages people on a protected ground, without objective justification.
Changes an employer makes so that a disabled employee can do the job, unless this would be a disproportionate burden.
A written document setting out an employer's safety and health arrangements, based on the risks identified at work.
A State body that investigates and decides many employment complaints and disputes.
An agreement on pay and conditions negotiated between a union and an employer, covering a group of workers.
A set sequence of steps by which an employee raises a complaint about their employment.

factCards.term: Nine grounds of discrimination under the Employment Equality Acts
factCards.definition: Gender, civil status, family status, sexual orientation, religion, age, disability, race, and membership of the Traveller community.

factCards.term: Employer duties under the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act
factCards.definition: Identify hazards, assess risks, prepare a safety statement, and provide training, information and safe equipment.

factCards.term: Employee duties under the same Act
factCards.definition: Take reasonable care of their own and others' safety, use protective equipment, and report hazards and accidents.
Capability, conduct, redundancy, a legal prohibition, or another substantial reason, applied with fair procedures.
The WRC investigates and adjudicates; the Labour Court hears appeals.
Legislation sets rights for all workers; contracts, collective agreements, handbooks and codes of practice add further protection.

questions.prompt: Discuss how legislation protects employees in relation to pay, working conditions and health and safety, and explain the role of the WRC in enforcing these rights.
questions.model: On pay, the National Minimum Wage Act 2000 sets a legal floor for hourly rates, and the Payment of Wages Act 1991 requires wages to be paid on time with a written statement of pay and deductions. On conditions, the Organisation of Working Time Act 1997 limits average working hours and guarantees rest breaks and annual leave, while the Sick Leave Act 2022 gives a right to paid sick leave. On health and safety, the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 requires employers to assess risks and provide training and safe equipment, and it requires employees to take reasonable care. The WRC enforces many of these rights by investigating complaints and deciding claims on pay, working time, discrimination and dismissal, with appeals going to the Labour Court.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between direct and indirect discrimination, and give an example of each in an Irish workplace.
questions.model: Direct discrimination occurs when a person is treated less favourably because of a protected ground, such as refusing to promote an employee because of their age. Indirect discrimination occurs when a rule that applies to everyone disadvantages people on a protected ground, such as requiring full-time evening shifts that make it very hard for a carer to take a job, unless the employer can show the rule is objectively justified.

questions.prompt: Outline two reasons why a dismissal may be fair, and explain what constructive dismissal means.
questions.model: A dismissal may be fair for capability, where an employee cannot do the job to the required standard, or for conduct, where an employee has breached discipline. Constructive dismissal occurs when an employee resigns because the employer's conduct makes continued employment unreasonable, and the law treats that resignation as a dismissal.
